challenges.opponent_argument: The mootness/waiver argument is too broad. The only authority the brief cites is the rule that satisfaction of judgment can moot an appeal, but the brief’s own chronology says the mechanic’s liens were released later by court order, not by Appellants’ voluntary satisfaction of the judgment. On the brief’s own facts, that is not the same thing as a voluntary satisfaction that would automatically extinguish appellate review.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the release of the liens does not moot the challenge, Appellants can still argue the merits of the judgment-on-the-pleadings ruling, and appellee loses an important threshold defense.

target.excerpt: THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY DECIDED APPELLEE'S MOTION FOR JUDGMENT ON THE PLEADINGS.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. The brief cites the mootness rule from Blodgett and Art's Rental, but the record facts it recites are not a voluntary satisfaction of judgment by Appellants; the mechanic's liens were later released by court order after no stay was obtained. That is a materially different posture, and the cited authority does not automatically convert a court-ordered release into mootness or waiver. If the court rejects mootness, Appellee loses its threshold defense to review of the JOP ruling.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants did not obtain a stay of the July 17, 2019 order, and the trial court later entered an order releasing the mechanic’s liens of record. Appellants therefore cannot undo the relief the court had already ordered and enforced. In any event, the trial court correctly granted judgment on the pleadings because the pleadings and admitted facts established that the liens were subject to the pending foreclosure and that no factual issue remained for trial.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not say the JOP issue is moot merely because the liens were later released of record. The supplied authorities do not establish that a court-ordered release after no stay is the same as voluntary satisfaction of judgment, so the safest course is to withdraw the mootness/waiver overstatement and argue the merits as an alternative.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even accepting the lien filings as false, the fraud claim still required justifiable reliance and resulting injury. The brief’s own facts say Appellee had no knowledge of Appellants’ alleged work until after Appellee acquired the property, which undercuts any claim that Appellee relied on Appellants’ alleged misrepresentations in entering the transaction or in suffering the alleged loss. A nonmovant’s failure to respond does not relieve the movant of proving every element with record evidence.
challenges.why_it_matters: If reliance is missing, the fraud judgment cannot stand as a matter of law, and summary judgment should be reversed at least on the fraud claim.

target.excerpt: THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY GRANTED APPELLEE'S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real weakness. Fraud under Ohio law requires justifiable reliance and resulting injury, and the brief's own timeline says Appellee had no knowledge of Appellants' claimed work until after it acquired the property. That undercuts any theory that Appellee relied on the false lien filings in entering the transaction. The brief gestures at reliance and injury, but it does not squarely bridge that element with record evidence. If the court accepts the attack, the fraud summary-judgment count is vulnerable even if the lien filings were false.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee’s fraud claim was based on Appellants’ false recorded mechanic’s-lien affidavits, which were filed against Appellee’s Property and were intended to mislead Appellee and others into believing that valid obligations existed and that the liens were enforceable. Appellee’s evidence showed that Appellants’ false filings clouded title, prevented clear transfer of the Property, and caused damages. Although Appellee learned of Appellants’ claimed work after acquiring the Property, the injury flowed from Appellants’ false public filings and the resulting cloud on title, and Appellants offered no contrary evidence on summary judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Add a direct, record-based explanation of how Appellee satisfied reliance and injury, or narrow the fraud discussion so it does not sound as though Appellee relied on the liens when it bought the Property. The present paragraph is too conclusory on that element.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief overstates what the recorded sheriff’s deed accomplishes. R.C. 5301.07 creates only a rebuttable presumption about a recorded real-property instrument; it does not itself define standing or marketable title. And the statute that actually describes who may bring a quiet-title action is R.C. 5303.01, which turns on possession or a claimed remainder/reversion interest—not simply on the existence of a recorded deed. The brief never bridges that statutory gap.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the court rejects the deed-as-standing shortcut, appellee’s standing theory loses its main foundation and the first assignment is no longer answered by the recording presumption alone.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a fair but not decisive attack. R.C. 5301.07 creates a presumption about a recorded real-property instrument; it does not itself define standing. But the brief does not rely on the statute alone. It also invokes the real-interest rule, judicial-sale cases, and the deed's recording before suit. On this record, the court is likely to view the quiet-title statute point as beside the main standing question rather than as a fatal gap.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee had standing because it acquired the Property at sheriff’s sale, the deed was recorded before suit, and the Recorder accepted that deed as a real-property instrument entitled to the statutory presumption of validity. See R.C. 2329.31 and 2329.36. Standing is measured at filing and turns on whether the party has a real interest in the subject matter of the action. State ex rel. Dallman v. Court of Common Pleas, 35 Ohio St. 2d 176, 179 (1973); Mousa v. Mount Carmel Health Sys., 2013-Ohio-2661, ¶ 12 (10th Dist.). Appellee also was in possession of the Property when the Complaint was filed. R.C. 5303.01 therefore supports Appellee’s quiet-title action, and R.C. 5301.07 confirms that the recorded deed was presumptively valid unless Appellants rebutted that presumption by clear and convincing evidence of fraud, duress, forgery, incompetency, or incapacity, which they did not do.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tie standing to the recorded sheriff’s deed, the sale-confirmation statutes, and Appellee’s possession, not to R.C. 5301.07 alone. If you keep the word "marketable title," use it only as support for the real-interest argument, not as a substitute for it.

challenges.opponent_argument: The slander-of-title theory is also underdeveloped. The cited authority requires malicious defamation of title and pecuniary damages. The brief points to false lien statements and to conclusory assertions about detriment to the property, but it does not identify evidence tying a specific pecuniary loss to the allegedly wrongful recordings themselves as opposed to the litigation process. Nor does it show, beyond conclusions, why the lien filings satisfy the malice requirement at the time of recording.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without proof of malice and pecuniary damages, the slander-of-title judgment is vulnerable even if the liens were inaccurate.

target.excerpt: THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY GRANTED APPELLEE'S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack is only partly persuasive. The brief does identify false lien statements, admissions that no contracts existed with two purported obligees, and evidence that the filings were reckless and intended to mislead. It also points to damages testimony. The complaint is that the briefing is conclusory, but on summary judgment the issue is whether the record evidence could support malice and pecuniary harm. On this record, the attack does not clearly defeat the slander-of-title claim.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee’s evidence supported slander of title. Appellants recorded three mechanic’s-lien affidavits asserting contracts with Realty Executives, Huntington National Bank, and the Pooles, yet they admitted they had no contract with Realty Executives or Huntington National Bank and failed to produce any contract with the Pooles. Those recorded false claims clouded title to the Property and caused pecuniary harm, as reflected in the damages evidence presented to the trial court and jury. Malice was shown by Appellants’ reckless disregard for Appellee’s rights when they filed and maintained recorded claims they knew were false or unsupported.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Strengthen slander of title by tying the false lien filings to the damages evidence and by emphasizing that malice can be inferred from knowingly false recordings, not from speculation. The present text should point to the admitted falsehoods and the damages testimony more explicitly.

challenges.opponent_argument: The punitive-damages submission is too loosely tied to actual malice. Under Preston, the court must have sufficient evidence that, when the challenged conduct occurred, the actor consciously disregarded a great probability of substantial harm. The brief relies heavily on Appellants’ hostile and combative conduct in the second phase of trial, but post-liability courtroom demeanor is not the same thing as evidence of actual malice at the time the liens were filed. That is a weak basis for sending punitive damages to the jury in the first place.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the record did not support actual malice at the time of the alleged wrong, the punitive-damages award is vulnerable regardless of the size of the award.

target.excerpt: V. THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY ALLOWED THE JURY TO DECIDE PUNITIVE DAMAGES AND THE JURY PROPERLY DECIDED THOSE DAMAGES.

challenges.judge_assessment: This point does not fully land because the brief does not rest punitive damages on hostile trial demeanor alone. It also relies on the knowingly false lien filings, admissions that key contract claims were false, and evidence of intent to mislead. Hostile second-phase conduct is not enough by itself, but the record described in the brief gives the jury a permissible malice inference. The more serious issue would be whether the trial court had sufficient evidence of actual malice from the underlying filings; the attack as framed misses that broader basis.
challenges.suggested_response: The punitive-damages submission was proper because the record contained evidence from which the jury could find actual malice before it ever considered Appellant Woods’ demeanor in the second phase of trial. Appellants filed false mechanic’s-lien affidavits, admitted they had no contract with two of the purported obligors, failed to produce a contract with the Pooles, and acted in reckless disregard of Appellee’s rights. That evidence alone supported an inference of hatred, ill will, or conscious disregard of a great probability of substantial harm under Preston v. Murty, and the later trial conduct merely confirmed the malice the jury was already entitled to find.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Make clear that punitive damages rested on the false filings and admissions, with the courtroom conduct only corroborating malice. Do not allow the argument to sound as though second-phase demeanor alone carried the issue to the jury.

challenges.opponent_argument: The judgment-on-the-pleadings analysis overreads lis pendens. The cited authorities say a later-acquired interest is taken subject to the pending action; they do not say the pendency of a foreclosure suit automatically establishes appellee’s right to quiet title on the pleadings without testing the underlying title issues. Under Civ.R. 12(C), the movant still must show that the nonmovant can prove no set of facts entitling relief. The brief treats lis pendens as dispositive of the entire title dispute, which is a stronger proposition than the authorities actually supply.
challenges.why_it_matters: If lis pendens is only notice and risk-shifting—not automatic title adjudication—then the pleadings may not have been enough to grant dispositive relief without further factual development.

target.excerpt: THE TRIAL COURT PROPERLY DECIDED APPELLEE'S MOTION FOR JUDGMENT ON THE PLEADINGS.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is not a strong reversal point on this record. The brief does more than say lis pendens exists; it ties the foreclosure filing date, the later mechanic's-lien dates, and the recorded deed together and cites authority that later-acquired interests take subject to the pending action. In that posture, lis pendens is being used as a title-priority rule, not as an all-purpose substitute for proof. The attack is accurate only to the extent lis pendens is notice, but it does not overcome the admitted timeline or the pleaded relief.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee does not contend that lis pendens alone proves title. Rather, the complaint, the recorded deed, and Appellants’ own admissions established the operative chronology: the foreclosure action was pending before Appellants’ first claimed work date, the sheriff’s deed had been recorded, and Appellants’ mechanic’s liens were filed after the lis pendens date. Under R.C. 2703.26 and the cases cited above, those later-acquired interests were taken subject to the pending foreclosure and could not defeat Appellee’s title. Because Appellants admitted the relevant dates and offered no contrary facts, the trial court properly determined that no factual issue remained and that Appellee was entitled to judgment on the pleadings.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede that lis pendens is notice and priority protection, then show why the pleadings plus Appellants’ admissions left no factual issue about the liens’ subordination to Appellee’s title. Do not present lis pendens as a substitute for title proof; present it as the rule that made the pleaded relief dispositive on these admitted facts.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief overstates what the recorded sheriff’s deed accomplishes. R.C. 5301.07 creates only a rebuttable presumption about a recorded real-property instrument; it does not itself define standing or marketable title. And the statute that actually describes who may bring a quiet-title action is R.C. 5303.01, which turns on possession or a claimed remainder/reversion interest—not simply on the existence of a recorded deed. The brief never bridges that statutory gap.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the court rejects the deed-as-standing shortcut, appellee’s standing theory loses its main foundation and the first assignment is no longer answered by the recording presumption alone.

attacks_proposed.argument: The mootness/waiver argument is too broad. The only authority the brief cites is the rule that satisfaction of judgment can moot an appeal, but the brief’s own chronology says the mechanic’s liens were released later by court order, not by Appellants’ voluntary satisfaction of the judgment. On the brief’s own facts, that is not the same thing as a voluntary satisfaction that would automatically extinguish appellate review.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the release of the liens does not moot the challenge, Appellants can still argue the merits of the judgment-on-the-pleadings ruling, and appellee loses an important threshold defense.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even accepting the lien filings as false, the fraud claim still required justifiable reliance and resulting injury. The brief’s own facts say Appellee had no knowledge of Appellants’ alleged work until after Appellee acquired the property, which undercuts any claim that Appellee relied on Appellants’ alleged misrepresentations in entering the transaction or in suffering the alleged loss. A nonmovant’s failure to respond does not relieve the movant of proving every element with record evidence.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If reliance is missing, the fraud judgment cannot stand as a matter of law, and summary judgment should be reversed at least on the fraud claim.

attacks_proposed.argument: The slander-of-title theory is also underdeveloped. The cited authority requires malicious defamation of title and pecuniary damages. The brief points to false lien statements and to conclusory assertions about detriment to the property, but it does not identify evidence tying a specific pecuniary loss to the allegedly wrongful recordings themselves as opposed to the litigation process. Nor does it show, beyond conclusions, why the lien filings satisfy the malice requirement at the time of recording.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof of malice and pecuniary damages, the slander-of-title judgment is vulnerable even if the liens were inaccurate.

attacks_proposed.argument: The punitive-damages submission is too loosely tied to actual malice. Under Preston, the court must have sufficient evidence that, when the challenged conduct occurred, the actor consciously disregarded a great probability of substantial harm. The brief relies heavily on Appellants’ hostile and combative conduct in the second phase of trial, but post-liability courtroom demeanor is not the same thing as evidence of actual malice at the time the liens were filed. That is a weak basis for sending punitive damages to the jury in the first place.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the record did not support actual malice at the time of the alleged wrong, the punitive-damages award is vulnerable regardless of the size of the award.

attacks_proposed.argument: The judgment-on-the-pleadings analysis overreads lis pendens. The cited authorities say a later-acquired interest is taken subject to the pending action; they do not say the pendency of a foreclosure suit automatically establishes appellee’s right to quiet title on the pleadings without testing the underlying title issues. Under Civ.R. 12(C), the movant still must show that the nonmovant can prove no set of facts entitling relief. The brief treats lis pendens as dispositive of the entire title dispute, which is a stronger proposition than the authorities actually supply.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If lis pendens is only notice and risk-shifting—not automatic title adjudication—then the pleadings may not have been enough to grant dispositive relief without further factual development.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands. The brief cites the mootness rule from Blodgett and Art's Rental, but the record facts it recites are not a voluntary satisfaction of judgment by Appellants; the mechanic's liens were later released by court order after no stay was obtained. That is a materially different posture, and the cited authority does not automatically convert a court-ordered release into mootness or waiver. If the court rejects mootness, Appellee loses its threshold defense to review of the JOP ruling.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says Appellants did not seek a stay or appeal the order and that the later release of the liens means the issues are now moot and/or waived; it also cites Blodgett and Art's Rental for the proposition that satisfaction of judgment moots appeal.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the lien release was voluntary satisfaction or purely a ministerial court-ordered release; whether any requested appellate relief survives the release.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a real weakness. Fraud under Ohio law requires justifiable reliance and resulting injury, and the brief's own timeline says Appellee had no knowledge of Appellants' claimed work until after it acquired the property. That undercuts any theory that Appellee relied on the false lien filings in entering the transaction. The brief gestures at reliance and injury, but it does not squarely bridge that element with record evidence. If the court accepts the attack, the fraud summary-judgment count is vulnerable even if the lien filings were false.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It recites the fraud elements, says false mechanic's-lien affidavits were recorded, and asserts that Appellee provided evidence that reliance on the recorded affidavits was justifiable and that damages were reasonably expected.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether Ohio recognizes reliance based on a false recording that affects title after purchase, and whether the record contains admissible evidence of justifiable reliance and proximate injury.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a fair but not decisive attack. R.C. 5301.07 creates a presumption about a recorded real-property instrument; it does not itself define standing. But the brief does not rely on the statute alone. It also invokes the real-interest rule, judicial-sale cases, and the deed's recording before suit. On this record, the court is likely to view the quiet-title statute point as beside the main standing question rather than as a fatal gap.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says standing is determined at commencement, a party has standing when it has a real interest in the subject matter, the sheriff's deed was recorded before suit, R.C. 5301.07 creates a presumption of validity, and the presumption was not rebutted.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether Ohio standing for these claims requires marketable title, possession, or only a recorded deed plus some real-property interest.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack is only partly persuasive. The brief does identify false lien statements, admissions that no contracts existed with two purported obligees, and evidence that the filings were reckless and intended to mislead. It also points to damages testimony. The complaint is that the briefing is conclusory, but on summary judgment the issue is whether the record evidence could support malice and pecuniary harm. On this record, the attack does not clearly defeat the slander-of-title claim.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says slander of title is wrongful recording of an unfounded claim causing pecuniary damage, cites cases on malice and wrongful lien filings, and asserts Appellee produced evidence of recklessness, intent to mislead, and damages.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The actual summary-judgment evidentiary materials showing the amount and causal chain of pecuniary loss attributable to the lien filings.

judge_assessments.assessment: This point does not fully land because the brief does not rest punitive damages on hostile trial demeanor alone. It also relies on the knowingly false lien filings, admissions that key contract claims were false, and evidence of intent to mislead. Hostile second-phase conduct is not enough by itself, but the record described in the brief gives the jury a permissible malice inference. The more serious issue would be whether the trial court had sufficient evidence of actual malice from the underlying filings; the attack as framed misses that broader basis.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says Ohio allows punitive damages on a showing of actual malice, cites Preston, Zoppo, Rice, and Bauer, and states that the jury could infer malice from Appellants' filings and conduct, not just from courtroom behavior.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the record contains evidence of conscious disregard at the time the liens were filed, separate from post-liability conduct.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is not a strong reversal point on this record. The brief does more than say lis pendens exists; it ties the foreclosure filing date, the later mechanic's-lien dates, and the recorded deed together and cites authority that later-acquired interests take subject to the pending action. In that posture, lis pendens is being used as a title-priority rule, not as an all-purpose substitute for proof. The attack is accurate only to the extent lis pendens is notice, but it does not overcome the admitted timeline or the pleaded relief.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It cites R.C. 2703.26, Wheeling, Bates, Cook, and Martin for the rule that later-acquired interests are subject to the pending foreclosure and that Appellants' liens were filed after the lis pendens date, making them void as against Appellee's title.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the pleadings and admissions alone were enough for judgment on the pleadings, and whether Ohio treats post-lis-pendens mechanic's liens as void against the foreclosure plaintiff as a matter of law.

results.verdict: Mixed: the brief is solid on the title-priority theory, but
results.assessment: As written, the brief has real footing on the lis pendens/recording chronology and on the punitive-damages and slander-of-title theories, but it is vulnerable where it leans on threshold doctrines and element proof. The biggest weakness is the mootness/waiver argument: the cited satisfaction-of-judgment rule does not neatly fit a court-ordered release of liens. The fraud summary-judgment section is also shaky because the timeline undercuts justifiable reliance and the brief does not fully bridge injury with record evidence. The standing attack is fair but not decisive, and the research did not reveal a settled fatal flaw beyond those points.

The cited fraud authorities do require justifiable reliance and proximate injury, and on this record the brief mostly points to false lien filings, false statements, and a conclusory assertion that appellee relied and was damaged. It does answer with the summary-judgment record and says appellants filed no timely opposition, but it does not cleanly identify a concrete transaction, reliance chain, or how the losses flowed from the alleged misrepresentations rather than from the foreclosure/lis pendens posture. challenges.suggested_response: Appellee's fraud claim was based on Appellants' knowingly false recorded affidavits, filed with the intent to mislead and to assert liens they had no basis to claim. Those false recordings injured Appellee by clouding title to the Property and forcing Appellee to litigate and obtain relief to clear the liens. Appellants cite no record evidence rebutting Appellee's summary-judgment showing on falsity, knowledge, intent, and injury. To the extent Appellants contend a more specific reliance citation was required, the brief should identify the record support establishing that element expressly.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: This point needs a concrete record citation for reliance or a candid narrowing of the fraud discussion. If the record does not identify a specific reliance event, do not overstate the fraud proof; instead, anchor the claim in the false recordings, their intent to mislead, and the injury from the cloud on title, while acknowledging that the brief should cite the exact evidence supporting reliance if it exists.

But hostility in court is not the same thing as actual malice in the underlying tort conduct, and the authorities cited in the retrieved materials do not permit punitive damages on mere frustration, posture, or courtroom demeanor. At most, the brief describes angry behavior; it does not establish the level of malice the law requires.
challenges.why_it_matters: If actual malice was not proven, the punitive award and any fee award tied to it should fall.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a legitimate attack, but the brief has more than hostile courtroom demeanor. It relies on the underlying false lien conduct, alleged knowledge of falsity, and conscious disregard, and it also notes the punitive instruction was not objected to. The problem is that the brief prominently uses Woods's combative behavior during the second phase as malice evidence, which is thinner than the governing actual-malice standard. On this record the court can still accept the broader malice theory, but the attack exposes that the punitive award is not well supported if the court isolates the trial-phase conduct from the underlying tort evidence.
challenges.suggested_response: The punitive-damages award was supported by Appellants' underlying conduct, not merely by their demeanor at trial. The record showed that Appellants filed recorded lien affidavits claiming contractual and monetary entitlement where they had no contract with Realty Executives or Huntington National Bank and produced no contract with the Pooles. From that conduct, the jury could find a conscious disregard for Appellee's rights sufficient to support punitive damages. Woods's combative conduct during the second phase of trial was additional evidence of malice, but not the sole basis for the award.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Recast the punitive-damages argument around the underlying false filings and admitted lack of contractual basis, not just Woods's courtroom demeanor. Make clear that the trial conduct was corroborative, not the sole proof of actual malice.

results.assessment: The brief is reasonably strong on standing, the lis pendens/priority theory, and the point that a late opposition does not defeat an otherwise supported summary judgment. Its main weakness is that the merits discussion of fraud and slander of title is too conclusory on the elements that matter most: it does not cleanly show justifiable reliance, proximate injury, or a tight causal link between the false recordings and the claimed losses. Punitive damages are also vulnerable because the brief leans too much on courtroom hostility instead of the underlying conduct. The November 16/17 discrepancy is real, but it reads more like a drafting flaw than a decisive defect.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a legitimate attack on the breadth of the standing fallback, but it overstates the collapse from 'not the named mortgagee' to 'no standing for any related damages.' The cited standing and real-party-in-interest authorities support the general prerequisite and the policy against duplicate suits; they do not, by themselves, prove that Lundberg can assert no personal claim at all. The brief partially answers by saying Equity Trust is the holder, not a party, no assignment or POA exists, and Lundberg is trying to invoke ownership only when helpful. The court could accept the narrower point that he is not the proper party to enforce the lien, but the broader 'no standing whatsoever' step is not fully established.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says Equity Trust is the mortgagee, Lundberg is not, standing is a prerequisite, no assignment or power of attorney was shown, and therefore Lundberg cannot sue to enforce the lien or seek damages flowing from it.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is only partly persuasive. judge_assessments.assessment: This is not a strong attack on the record provided. The brief's procedural point is simple: the sur-reply arguments were in filings the trial court struck, and the striking orders were not assigned as error. That is the ordinary kind of preservation problem an Ohio appellate court can enforce without a special citation in the brief. The cited materials about appeal perfection and objections do not directly undermine that. Land Title loses little here unless the appellate court decides to overlook preservation and reach the stricken arguments anyway.

results.assessment: The brief has a usable proximate-cause narrative because it ties the claimed lack of injury to the signed release and the parties’ later arrangement, and the standing point has some force to the extent it says Lundberg is not the proper party to enforce rights belonging to Equity Trust. But the brief is vulnerable on the core issue: it does not cleanly establish that Lundberg had authority to bind the actual mortgagee, and its apparent-authority fallback is weak because it points to Lundberg’s conduct rather than the principal’s. The record disputes over signature and authorization are not fully answered, and the brief’s broad standing move overreaches beyond what the cited authorities plainly support.

results.assessment: The brief is not fully persuasive as written: its proximate-cause theory has some force because it ties the claimed injury to Lundberg’s own release-and-unsecured arrangement, but it overreaches in treating standing as categorically barred and in brushing aside disputed mortgage, notarization, and release facts as immaterial. challenges.judge_assessment: The stay-and-supersedeas authorities do not directly undermine mootness from an already executed judgment. They show how a party can preserve the status quo before execution, but they do not say an appeal remains live after execution has occurred and the appellant concedes satisfaction of the judgment. challenges.suggested_response: Appellants' stay authorities do not help them. Aultman, BancPlus Mortgage, Lachance, and the treatise materials address how a party may preserve the status quo pending appeal by obtaining a stay or supersedeas bond before execution. They do not hold that an appeal remains live after the judgment has already been executed and satisfied. Here, Lender recorded and thereby executed the judgment before Appellants appealed or sought a stay, and Appellants concede that fact. Because the relief they seek would not undo what has already been done, the appeal presents no live controversy and is academic.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the mootness point, but narrow it. challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. The cited stay/supersedeas sources, especially the post-execution reference to R.C. 1923.14 in Bowling Green Manor, undercut any categorical statement that an executed judgment always eliminates appellate relief. On this record, the mootness theory is vulnerable because the judgment was recorded, but the brief's waiver point is still a real obstacle: it says the Stovalls did not challenge mootness in their jurisdictional memorandum and that the Court does not consider issues not raised there. If the Court reaches the merits of mootness, the advocate risks losing the dismissal ground; if the Court enforces waiver, the attack only partly helps.
challenges.suggested_response: A. The Stovalls do not meaningfully challenge the Eighth District's mootness ruling. Their memorandum asks this Court to reach the merits despite the fact that Lender recorded a certified copy of the judgment before the notice of appeal and before any stay, and the trial court later denied a stay as moot because Lender had already executed judgment. See Mem. at 2. In any event, the only issues the Stovalls raise are merits questions about summary judgment, not any question of public and great general interest or any substantial constitutional question. And this Court does not consider issues that a party failed to raise in its jurisdictional memorandum. Corporex Dev. & Constr. Mgt., Inc. v. Shook, Inc., 2005-Ohio-5409, ¶ 5, fn. 1. Because the issues the Stovalls raise would not change the outcome below, this appeal would be purely academic. See State ex rel. Cincinnati Enquirer v. Hunter, 2014-Ohio-5457, ¶ 4, citing In re L.W., 2006-Ohio-644, ¶ 11 (10th Dist.).
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise the mootness discussion so it does not claim, categorically, that an executed judgment always ends appellate relief. Keep the waiver point front and center, and frame mootness as the basis on which the Eighth District dismissed this appeal, not as a universal rule this Court must adopt.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack does not land well on this record. Ohio Rule 56 requires competent evidence, but the brief expressly says Lender supported summary judgment with affidavits and properly authenticated exhibits, while the Stovalls offered no evidentiary countershowing and no sworn statement. The cited hearsay authority does not identify a concrete defect in Lender's proof; it only states that some affidavits in eviction cases can be hearsay when objected to and inadmissible for that reason. Without a specific admissibility problem, the attack is speculative. The advocate loses the chance to reopen the merits, but only if a court accepts the brief's characterization of the record as entirely one-sided.
challenges.suggested_response: The first three arguments challenge the admissibility and sufficiency of Lender's summary-judgment evidence. But Lender met her initial burden under Civ.R. 56 by submitting affidavits and other evidence properly authenticated by attached affidavit. See Civ.R. 56(C), (E); see also CMHA v. Barry Gauntt et al., 2014 CVG 001938 (summarizing the moving party's burden and the nonmoving party's reciprocal duty to set forth specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial). The Stovalls, by contrast, identified no concrete defect in Lender's proof and submitted no evidence in response--not even a sworn statement from either Appellant. Bare assertions that an affidavit is 'false' or was not tested on cross-examination do not create a genuine issue of material fact.

results.verdict: persuasive in parts but vulnerable on the mootness and merit
results.assessment: The brief reads strongest on waiver and on the basic summary-judgment record: it clearly says the Stovalls did not raise the right issues in their jurisdictional memorandum, and it presents Lender’s proof as affidavits and authenticated exhibits with no counterevidence from the Stovalls. The weak spots are the categorical mootness language and the due-process response. The challenges show Ohio authority does not support treating execution of judgment as automatically ending appellate relief, so the brief overstates that point, and the due-process section answers too broadly by relying on the Stovalls’ failure to participate rather than the adequacy of the procedure itself. The research did not leave a clearer opening on the summary-judgment admissibility issue without a specific defect in Lender’s evidence.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real pressure point because the brief itself concedes there was then a certified conflict over whether SB 97 could be incorporated during a guaranteed-renewal period. But on this record the brief also has dates and Ohio appellate authority (Arn, Advent, St. Clair) supporting Westport's renewal analysis. The attack does not show the court must reject that line as a matter of law; it shows the issue was contested. Westport risks losing only if this panel treats the conflict as defeating summary judgment rather than following the authorities Westport cites.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if the panel views the renewal-incorporation question as one on which appellate districts disagreed, the undisputed dates in this record still control: SB 97 was effective before the policy renewed on January 1, 2002, and Arn, Advent, and St. Clair support application of the amended statute at renewal. The later certified conflict in Advent shows the issue was debated, not that the trial court lacked authority to apply the amended statute on this record. Under the dates before this Court, Ohio law in effect at the January 1, 2002 renewal did not require Westport to offer UM/UIM coverage, and coverage cannot be implied as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not concede that the certified conflict defeats summary judgment. Reframe the point as an application of the authorities Westport already cites to the undisputed January 1, 2002 renewal, while acknowledging that Advent later noted a conflict but did not change the controlling dates in this record.

challenges.judge_assessment: Same basic vulnerability as a1, but narrower. The brief does not merely assume January 1, 2002 mattered; it ties that date to the quoted rule that statutory changes may be incorporated at renewal and to Arn's treatment of a February 2002 renewal after SB 97. The attack is fair in saying the renewal mechanics are the hard part, but it does not defeat the brief on this record because the brief already supplies the legal hook it needs. Westport's downside is that if the court reads Storer/Shay as limiting mid-period incorporation, this argument collapses.
challenges.suggested_response: Westport does not assume that every statutory amendment automatically enters a policy midstream. Rather, the record shows the policy renewed on January 1, 2002, after SB 97 became effective, and the authorities Westport cites hold that statutory changes may be incorporated at renewal and that the law in effect at the renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage. Plaintiffs identify no policy language or renewal mechanic in this record that prevents the January 1, 2002 renewal from incorporating SB 97. On this record, the amended statute governed the policy when the loss occurred.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Add a sentence tying the January 1, 2002 renewal to the policy's renewal mechanics and make clear you are not assuming automatic incorporation; you are relying on the renewal authorities already cited. If you want a broader proposition than those authorities support, you need more authority.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport's excess-policy argument is too thin. The Commercial Excess Policy is described as a separate policy that provides sums in excess of primary insurance and retained limits. Westport cannot collapse that separate coverage grant into the auto policy and then declare the excess form outside R.C. 3937.18 without analyzing the excess policy itself. A 'follows form' description is not the same thing as proving statutory inapplicability or proving that the excess layer can never support UM/UIM coverage.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the excess policy is a separate liability policy, Westport's blanket exclusion of it from the UM/UIM analysis fails.

target.excerpt: 3) The Commercial Excess Policy is not required to provide UM/UIM coverage where there is no such coverage under the underlying Auto and General Liability policies.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a legitimate attack because the excess policy is a separate layer of coverage and the brief's treatment is mostly conclusory. The record shows the excess policy has its own grant of coverage, even if it follows form on automobile liability terms, and the brief cites no authority squarely holding that an excess/umbrella form can never independently trigger UM/UIM obligations. Still, the brief does say the excess policy tracks the primary auto policy and extends only above primary insurance or a retained limit, so the argument is not unanswered. Westport stands to lose if the court treats the excess policy as an independently issued motor-vehicle liability policy rather than as a purely derivative layer.
challenges.suggested_response: The Commercial Excess Policy is not being treated as an independent source of UM/UIM coverage on this record. Westport identified it as an excess layer that provides sums above the primary insurance and that follows the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the underlying auto policy for automobile liability. Plaintiffs have pointed to no separate UM/UIM grant in the excess form and no authority requiring a separate UM/UIM analysis where the underlying auto policy is not subject to R.C. 3937.18. Accordingly, the excess policy does not alter the summary-judgment result here.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the excess-policy point to the follow-form nature of the layer and avoid an absolute statement that no excess policy can ever implicate UM/UIM coverage. If you want that broader rule, you need a case or policy text showing it.

The quoted statutory text does remove any mandatory-offer requirement for qualifying policies, and the brief ties its no-implied-coverage point to Arn and the renewal date. The attack correctly notes that the statutory text alone does not resolve the renewal issue, but the brief does not rely on the text alone; it pairs the text with renewal-case authority and the January 1, 2002 renewal facts. The point is answerable, not fatal. Westport would lose only if the court rejects its renewal analysis and reads SB 97 as inapplicable to the policy period.
challenges.suggested_response: The amended text of R.C. 3937.18 did more than remove a mandatory-offer requirement; under Arn, Advent, and St. Clair, it governed the scope of UM/UIM coverage at renewal. Here, the policy renewed on January 1, 2002, after SB 97 became effective, so the amended statute applied when the policy in effect on the date of loss was issued. Under that law, Westport had no duty to offer UM/UIM coverage, and no such coverage can be implied by operation of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue the statutory text alone resolves the case; tie the amended text to the renewal date and the renewal cases, and concede only that the issue was contested before the courts. The safe point is that, under the authorities Westport cites, SB 97 applied at the January 1, 2002 renewal and eliminated any implied UM/UIM coverage.

Westport's conclusion that UM/UIM 'can no longer be implied as a matter of law' depends entirely on resolving the renewal-incorporation issue in its favor, and that issue was not settled beyond dispute in the authorities it cites.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If SB97 does not conclusively resolve how the renewal period operates, Westport's no-implied-coverage argument is incomplete.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a real pressure point because the brief itself concedes there was then a certified conflict over whether SB 97 could be incorporated during a guaranteed-renewal period. But on this record the brief also has dates and Ohio appellate authority (Arn, Advent, St. Clair) supporting Westport's renewal analysis. The attack does not show the court must reject that line as a matter of law; it shows the issue was contested. Westport risks losing only if this panel treats the conflict as defeating summary judgment rather than following the authorities Westport cites.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It quotes Arn, Advent, and St. Clair for the proposition that statutory changes may be incorporated at renewal, says SB 97 became effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal, and states that at the July 15, 2002 loss Ohio law no longer required UM/UIM offers and such coverage could not be implied.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A merits decision would turn on which renewal/incorporation cases were controlling in the Eighth District at the time and whether the certified conflict had already undercut reliance on those cases.

judge_assessments.assessment: Same basic vulnerability as a1, but narrower. The brief does not merely assume January 1, 2002 mattered; it ties that date to the quoted rule that statutory changes may be incorporated at renewal and to Arn's treatment of a February 2002 renewal after SB 97. The attack is fair in saying the renewal mechanics are the hard part, but it does not defeat the brief on this record because the brief already supplies the legal hook it needs. Westport's downside is that if the court reads Storer/Shay as limiting mid-period incorporation, this argument collapses.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It states the policies renewed on January 1, 2002, quotes R.C. 3937.18(E), and argues that under Advent, McDaniel, Arn, and St. Clair, statutory changes could be incorporated at renewal and SB 97 therefore governed the policy on the date of loss.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Controlling authority on how SB 97 interacts with guaranteed renewals and whether renewal, not original issuance, governs UM/UIM obligations.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a legitimate attack because the excess policy is a separate layer of coverage and the brief's treatment is mostly conclusory. The record shows the excess policy has its own grant of coverage, even if it follows form on automobile liability terms, and the brief cites no authority squarely holding that an excess/umbrella form can never independently trigger UM/UIM obligations. Still, the brief does say the excess policy tracks the primary auto policy and extends only above primary insurance or a retained limit, so the argument is not unanswered. Westport stands to lose if the court treats the excess policy as an independently issued motor-vehicle liability policy rather than as a purely derivative layer.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says the Commercial Excess Policy provides sums in excess of primary insurance and retained limits, is subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the primary auto policy for automobile liability, and therefore covers the same out-of-state vehicles; it also says the excess policy is not required to provide UM/UIM coverage where the underlying policies do not.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Authority on whether a follow-form commercial excess/umbrella policy can carry UM/UIM obligations independent of the underlying auto policy under Ohio law.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack has some rhetorical force, but it does not land strongly on this record. The brief says the December 1, 2000 period was evidenced by a binder and that Westport produced the later policy forms and the binder; it then argues plaintiffs cite no authority for implying UM/UIM coverage from nonproduction. The attack's premise that the binder or inception-period terms were not produced is not shown by the record excerpts here, and the brief already answers the production complaint directly. Westport loses little unless plaintiffs can identify a specific unproduced controlling form and explain why it matters legally.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It states there was no physically printed policy for December 1, 2000 to January 1, 2001, but a binder evidenced that coverage and the January 1, 2001 and January 1, 2002 policies were produced; it also says plaintiffs offered no legal support for implying UM/UIM coverage from nonproduction.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Whether the binder was the operative contract and whether any truly controlling inception-period form differs from the later produced forms.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is largely a repackaging of a1 and a2. The quoted statutory text does remove any mandatory-offer requirement for qualifying policies, and the brief ties its no-implied-coverage point to Arn and the renewal date. The attack correctly notes that the statutory text alone does not resolve the renewal issue, but the brief does not rely on the text alone; it pairs the text with renewal-case authority and the January 1, 2002 renewal facts. The point is answerable, not fatal. Westport would lose only if the court rejects its renewal analysis and reads SB 97 as inapplicable to the policy period.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It quotes the amended R.C. 3937.18(A) language that a policy 'may, but is not required to' include UM/UIM coverage and then says Arn holds that at the February 21, 2002 renewal State Farm did not have to offer or include UM/UIM coverage and such coverage could no longer be implied by operation of law.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The decisive issue is not the statutory wording in the abstract, but whether the January 1, 2002 renewal legally brought the amended statute into the policy.

results.verdict: serviceable but exposed on the renewal-incorporation issue a
results.assessment: The brief has real support in the dates and in the authorities it cites, so it is not flimsy as written, but its weakest point is the January 1, 2002 renewal theory: the challenge shows Westport leans hard on a contested incorporation question and does not fully answer the guaranteed-renewal objection. The excess-policy section is also too conclusory; it treats a separate coverage layer as derivative without enough analysis of that policy itself. The nonproduction point is stronger, though it still needs a tighter explanation of why any missing controlling form matters. The research confirms the dispute was debated, but it does not eliminate the need to shore up the renewal mechanics.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands as a real but not dispositive challenge. The brief itself concedes a certified conflict between Advent and Storer, so the renewal/SB97 question was not settled law at the time. That means Westport cannot present this ground as unassailable. But the attack does not defeat the brief outright on this record because an Ohio appellate court could still decide the issue under its own precedent, distinguish the cases, or affirm on Westport's separate no-R.C. 3937.18 ground.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants’ reliance on the pre-SB97 law does not defeat summary judgment. The record reflects that the Westport coverage was renewed on January 1, 2001 and again on January 1, 2002, and Westport’s position is that the law in effect at the time of renewal governed the scope of any UM/UIM coverage. See Arn v. McLean, Advent v. Allstate Insurance Company, and St. Clair v. Allstate Insurance Company. Although appellants note that the Advent/Storer question was the subject of a certified conflict, that does not create a genuine issue of material fact on this record, and it does not undermine the separate and independent ground that R.C. 3937.18 does not apply to these policies in the first instance.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the SB97 discussion so it is framed as an additional basis for affirmance, not the sole answer to appellants’ theory. Acknowledge the conflict only to the extent necessary, then rely primarily on the uncontested renewal dates and the cases Westport cites that treat the law in effect at renewal as controlling.

challenges.why_it_matters: If the policy text does not show the claimed renewal effect, Westport’s timing argument cannot defeat coverage as a matter of law.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a legitimate criticism of the excess-policy argument. Westport asserts the excess form need not provide UM/UIM coverage because the underlying auto and general liability policies do not, but the brief does not cite separate excess-policy authority and does not quote the umbrella language in enough detail to show the layer could not stand alone. challenges.suggested_response: The Commercial Excess Policy does not create a separate basis for UM/UIM coverage. By its terms, it provides sums in excess of primary insurance or a retained limit, and it is subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the primary automobile coverage. Because the underlying automobile policy is not subject to R.C. 3937.18, and because the excess form follows the primary coverage rather than expanding it, the Commercial Excess Policy likewise does not require UM/UIM coverage.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Strengthen the excess-policy point by grounding it in the policy language already summarized in the record: the excess form provides only coverage above primary insurance or a retained limit and is subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the primary auto coverage.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. R.C. 5303.08 requires that the claimant have obtained title and be in quiet possession without fraud or collusion, and the brief’s own facts sound in an executory purchase arrangement and a deed held in escrow—not clearly in title actually obtained. The brief tries to recast Solomon as an equitable owner, but the cited statute and the narrow-construction authority the opposition would cite cut against that move. On this record, the court could reject the occupying-claimant theory without reaching damages.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 5303.08 applies only where the claimant, without fraud or collusion, has obtained title and is in quiet possession. The record shows that Solomon occupied the property under a series of purchase agreements, made improvements, and had a deed placed in escrow, but it does not establish that title was actually conveyed to him. Accordingly, Solomon cannot rely on the occupying-claimant statute as an independent ground for possession on the present record.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not overstate R.C. 5303.08. The statute requires title actually obtained and quiet possession without fraud or collusion, and the record as supplied does not show that Solomon received title; it shows an executory purchase arrangement and a deed placed in escrow. If you cannot add record support showing title passed, this assignment should be narrowed or abandoned as an independent basis for relief.

The brief partially answers this by saying Mustafa could not take an interest superior to Solomon and by characterizing the deed as fraudulent/no rights, but it still presses farther than the quoted authorities comfortably go. challenges.suggested_response: Under R.C. 2703.26 and Cook v. Mozer, the pending action charged Mustafa with notice, and any interest acquired during the litigation was subject to the final adjudication of Solomon’s claim. The record further reflects that CHT advised Horvath that Solomon’s rights “may” exist and that a title policy for Mustafa would have to be subject to those rights. On this record, Mustafa could not obtain a position superior to Solomon’s pending interest, and the trial court therefore erred in entering summary judgment in Mustafa’s favor before Solomon’s claim was adjudicated.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow this assignment to the point the authorities actually support: a transferee during pending litigation takes subject to the outcome of the case. Do not press the deed as automatically void ab initio unless you have authority for that proposition; the safer ask is that summary judgment for Mustafa was improper because his interest could not cut off Solomon’s pending claim.

challenges.judge_assessment: Ohio’s general American-rule cases do support the point that attorney fees are not automatically jury-determined and usually require statutory or contractual authorization. results.assessment: The brief reads as partially persuasive, but its weakest point is the occupying-claimant theory: the record as summarized does not show that Solomon actually obtained title, so that argument is vulnerable to outright rejection. The lis pendens and derivative-mortgage sections have more force, yet they still press beyond what the cited authorities comfortably establish; they support notice and subordination more readily than automatic invalidation of later deeds or liens. The jury/fee argument is also overstated and needs narrowing. Overall, the brief can still work if it tightens the relief sought and separates status, notice, and damages theories more carefully.

challenges.opponent_argument: Civ.R. 52 does not require findings of fact and conclusions of law on a summary-judgment ruling. The trial court's refusal to issue them was therefore not reversible error merely because Harwood asked for them.
challenges.why_it_matters: If no findings were required, this assignment of error fails outright and cannot justify reversal or remand.

queries: Ohio Civ.R. 52 findings of fact conclusions of law summary judgment not required request denied no reversible error Ohio appellate cases

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the cleanest procedural attack. Ohio authority the brief ignores points the other way: Civ.R. 52 findings are not ordinarily required for a summary-judgment ruling, so denial of the request is not reversible merely because Harwood asked. On this record, the brief says only that the order was 'potentially final' and that findings were 'required,' but it does not supply authority making Civ.R. 52 mandatory here.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants preserve this assignment only to the extent the trial court entered dispositive rulings affecting multiple claims without explaining the factual and legal basis for each ruling. Otherwise, Appellants acknowledge that they have not supplied authority in this record establishing that Civ.R. 52 required findings of fact and conclusions of law on these summary-judgment rulings.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not press this as a standalone reversal point unless you can add Ohio authority that Civ.R. 52 requires findings after summary judgment in this posture. On the present record, the safer course is to narrow the point to lack of reviewable explanation, not a categorical entitlement to findings.

challenges.opponent_argument: The malpractice claim against Horvath is built on inference, not a developed Scholler showing. The brief identifies no attorney-client relationship between Horvath and Solomon, and its malice theory is just a repackaging of the same disputed business deal: competing contracts, termination of a transaction, and concealment allegations. That is not the same as proving legal-malpractice malice as opposed to adverse representation in a real-estate dispute.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without a real privity showing or evidence of malice beyond the contract dispute itself, the malpractice claim cannot survive summary judgment.

target.excerpt: V.  THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT TO HORVATH WHERE SOLOMON SATISFIED BOTH THE PRIVITY AND MALICE PRONGS OF SCHOLLER, THE QUESTION OF WHETHER MALICE EXISTED WAS A JURY ISSUE. AND SOLOMON PROVIDED EXPERT TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF HIS LEGAL MALPRACTICE CLAIM.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attacks a core element of the malpractice theory. The brief stretches Scholler by treating Solomon's contract with Harwood as enough 'privity' with Horvath's client, and then recasts a business-dispute fact pattern as malice. That is vulnerable in an Ohio court: if the court rejects the privity shortcut or sees only adverse representation in a real-estate deal, the malpractice claim falls. The brief does answer with Macken and its malice discussion, but the answer is not especially robust.
challenges.suggested_response: Solomon's malpractice claim does not depend on an attorney-client relationship between Solomon and Horvath. Under Scholler, a third person may proceed where the attorney acts maliciously, and the summary-judgment record permits that inference here: Horvath knew of Solomon's contract, communicated the extension, then executed or advanced the Mustafa transaction while Solomon's rights remained outstanding. At minimum, whether Horvath acted with the requisite malice is a question for the trier of fact, and the expert testimony offered by Solomon supports that claim if the facts are believed.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten the malpractice argument around the actual Scholler exception the brief invokes: malicious conduct. Do not overstate direct privity with Horvath; instead, anchor the claim in the evidence that Horvath knowingly acted against Solomon's interests while representing Harwood.

challenges.opponent_argument: Solomon never supplies competent proof that he actually could have closed by December 14. Gill's affidavit was later undercut by his deposition, where he said he still needed loan documentation, had not completed due diligence, and could not say he would have been certain to make the loan in 24 hours. That is not enough to create a genuine issue on ability to perform.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without proof that Solomon was ready, willing, and able to close, the anticipatory-breach/specific-performance theory fails at a core element.

target.excerpt: III.  THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT TO APPELLEES WHERE GENUINE ISSUES OF FACT AND CREDIBILITY EXISTED REGARDING WHETHER HARWOOD HAD ANTICIPATORILY BREACHED THE PURCHASE AGREEMENT. AND WHETHER SOLOMON HAD FINANCING TO PURCHASE THE PROPERTY AND COULD HAVE CLOSED SUCH TRANSACTION H

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real summary-judgment attack, but the brief is not silent on it. It points to Gill's affidavit saying he was willing and able to close if the loan conditions were met, then spends pages arguing that Gill's later testimony is internally inconsistent and goes to credibility for the jury. On this record, the appellate court will not weigh credibility, so the attack is not automatically fatal; it becomes serious only if the court treats Gill's deposition as conclusively negating ability to perform.
challenges.suggested_response: Solomon produced evidence that Gill was willing and able to fund the purchase if the loan conditions were met and that he remained 'ready, willing and able if we had gotten over these hurdles.' The later deposition and notes do not eliminate that showing as a matter of law; they create a credibility dispute that cannot be resolved on summary judgment. A trier of fact must decide whether Solomon could have closed by December 14, 2007 absent Harwood's termination of the contract the day before.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the argument focused on genuine factual dispute, not on proving ability to close as an undisputed fact. The record support is strongest if you rely on Gill's affidavit, his 'ready, willing and able' testimony, and the credibility conflicts with his later deposition and notes.

challenges.opponent_argument: The jury-right argument overstates Ohio law. The authority the brief invokes on attorney-fee awards reflects that fee amounts are determined by the court under reasonableness standards; it does not establish that every fee request becomes a jury question simply because one side labels it compensatory damages. The blanket demand for a jury determination of all damages is therefore too broad.
challenges.why_it_matters: If fee amounts are for the court, the denial of a jury on that issue is not reversible error.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack has support in the fee-damages authority the brief cites against itself: the fee amount question is ordinarily for the court under reasonableness standards, not automatically a jury issue. The brief does try to convert fee requests into compensatory damages and relies on Stonehenge and Keal, but those cases do not cleanly establish a blanket jury right for every fee request. This attack would likely narrow, though not necessarily eliminate, the damages/jury assignment.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not contend that every attorney-fee question is automatically for the jury. Rather, where Harwood and Resource sought fees and expenses as part of the damages flowing from the disputed transaction, the factual predicates for those awards were themselves contested and could not be removed from the jury on summary judgment. At a minimum, the trial court was required to submit the underlying damages issues to the jury before any fee-related award could be entered.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the jury-right argument. Do not claim every fee request is automatically for the jury; instead, argue that the disputed factual predicates for damages, including any fee component treated as part of compensatory relief, had to be tried and could not be decided summarily.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even on the brief's own rule, lis pendens is a notice-and-priority doctrine; it preserves the status quo and makes a later transferee take subject to the pending action. It does not, by itself, make Mustafa's deed or RSB's mortgages void ab initio. The brief overreaches when it asks for wholesale invalidation of title rather than a subject-to-the-outcome ruling.
challenges.why_it_matters: If lis pendens only preserves priority, not nullity, the requested reversal against Mustafa and RSB goes too far as a matter of law.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real overreach problem. Lis pendens preserves the status quo and ordinarily makes a later transferee take subject to the action; it does not, by itself, make the later deed void ab initio. The brief partially answers by saying Mustafa took subject to Solomon's rights, but it also uses language about fraudulent deeds and 'no rights,' which gives the appellees room to argue the requested relief goes too far. The attack would likely limit the remedy more than defeat the entire issue.
challenges.suggested_response: The relief sought is not a declaration that the later deed and mortgages are void in the abstract. Under Cook, Dickerson, and Levin, the point is narrower and sufficient: once this action was pending, any later transferee took subject to Solomon's claim, including his request for specific performance and the related equitable relief. Mustafa therefore could not acquire an interest superior to Solomon's pending rights, and the mortgages derived from that transfer are likewise subject to the outcome of this case.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede the doctrine's real scope and avoid asking for nullity unless you can support it. The better position is that Mustafa and any later mortgagee took subject to Solomon's pending claim, so the trial court should not have treated those later interests as superior to Solomon's rights.

challenges.opponent_argument: The escrow-breach theory is contradicted by the brief's own chronology. On December 13, Resource was told the closing deadline had been extended; the parties then agreed that if Solomon had not deposited the funds by 2:00 p.m. on December 14, Resource would return the money. Resource did exactly that. The record as presented shows a contested cutoff and compliance with the cutoff, not an 'unequivocal' breach.
challenges.why_it_matters: If Resource followed the parties' own instruction, the claims for fiduciary breach, contract breach, and negligence collapse.

target.excerpt: IV.  THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN ENFORCING INDEMNIFICATION AGREEMENT LANGUAGE IN RESOURCE'S STANDARD CONDITIONS OF ESCROW WHERE THE EVIDENCE ESTABLISHED UNEQUIVOCALLY THAT RESOURCE BREACHED ITS FIDUCIARY DUTY AND CONTRACTUAL RESPONSIBILITIES TO SOLOMON TO ASSIST HARWOOD IN AVOIDING HIS CONTRACTUAL OBLI

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a factual-record attack on the escrow-breach theory, and the brief does meet it head-on. The brief says Resource was told the closing was extended to December 14, that Horvath gave Resource conflicting directions, and that Resource terminated escrow at 2:00 p.m. without explanation or further communication. The appellees' best answer is that the parties agreed to the 2:00 p.m. cutoff and Resource simply followed instruction. On this record, that is a genuine factual dispute rather than an easy affirmance.
challenges.suggested_response: The escrow-breach claim turns on a factual dispute, not a one-sided record. The evidence before the court showed that Horvath confirmed to Resource that Solomon had until the close of business on December 14, 2007, while Resource then received inconsistent instructions and terminated the escrow without further communication with Solomon or Lynch. Whether Resource acted loyally, carefully, and in accordance with the parties' instructions was therefore a question for the trier of fact, not summary judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the answer on the summary-judgment standard and the conflicting instructions to Resource. Do not characterize Resource's conduct as undisputedly wrongful; instead, show why the cutoff and the termination instructions were genuinely disputed and therefore could not be resolved against Solomon as a matter of law.

challenges.opponent_argument: The blanket request to vacate all damages awards and punitive damages is overbroad. The brief assumes every award is purely derivative of the challenged liability rulings, but it does not separately analyze each award or show that each one necessarily falls if only some liability issues are altered. That is not a sufficient appellate showing for sweeping relief.
challenges.why_it_matters: Even if the Court disagrees with one liability ruling, the damages awards do not automatically collapse without a separate showing as to each award.

target.excerpt: X.  THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN AWARDING DAMAGES TO APPELLEES HARWOOD, RESOURCE AND MUSTAFA. AND ALL SUCH AWARDS MUST BE VACATED.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is mostly an overbreadth objection, not a knockdown point. If some liability rulings are reversed, derivative damages awards often fall with them; the brief's blanket wording is imprecise, but the remedy request is not legally impossible. The stronger point is that punitive damages and any fee awards may need independent analysis, which the brief does not really supply. That said, this attack does not by itself defeat the damages assignment.
challenges.suggested_response: Because the damages awards rest on the liability determinations challenged in this appeal, those awards must be vacated to the extent they are derivative of the erroneous rulings on liability. Appellants do not seek broader relief than the law permits, but they do seek reversal of the compensatory, fee, cost, and punitive components that cannot stand once the underlying liability findings are reversed or remanded.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the request for relief to the awards that necessarily depend on the challenged liability rulings. Do not ask the court to vacate every award regardless of basis; ask for vacatur of the derivative awards and any punitive component that lacks an independent lawful predicate.

results.verdict: partly persuasive but exposed on the procedural and malpract
results.assessment: The brief has some real force where it relies on genuine factual disputes, especially the escrow-breach and financing-performance issues, and it can credibly argue that derivative damages should fall if liability is reversed. But it is vulnerable in three important places: the Civ.R. 52 point is weak because the record supplied does not show findings were required on summary judgment; the malpractice theory is thin because it stretches Scholler and repackages a business dispute as malice; and the lis pendens argument overreaches in the relief sought by sounding broader than a subject-to-the-action theory. The record-based disputes are the brief’s best material, but the legal framing needs tightening.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. On this record, the brief never supplies authority showing that Appellee's actual knowledge of Wilson's possession is an essential element of the underlying claims. The cited summary-judgment cases govern burdens, but the brief itself supplies only the conclusory premise that knowledge is material. A court can reject the argument for failing to tie the alleged factual dispute to a legally essential element.
challenges.suggested_response: The issue is not whether Appellee's knowledge of Wilson's possession is an independent element of Appellants' claim. Rather, it is the material fact that bears directly on waiver and estoppel: Appellee's own affidavit states that Ruth Gross became aware Dr. Todd Wilson had entered into possession of the subject premises, and the record further reflects that Appellee accepted rent from Wilson or his corporation. That evidence creates a genuine issue of material fact precluding summary judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Delete the claim that Appellee's actual knowledge of Wilson's possession is itself an essential element. Reframe knowledge as the material fact that supports waiver and estoppel, not as a standalone element you must prove.

challenges.opponent_argument: Appellants overstate Civ.R. 56. Under Dresher/Vahila, the moving party does not have to disprove every conceivable fact issue or use magic words such as "there is no genuine issue as to any material fact". It satisfies its initial burden by pointing to record material showing the absence of evidence on an essential element, after which the nonmovant must come forward with specific facts. The brief’s criticism that Appellee did not expressly negate knowledge is therefore not a Civ.R. 56 defect.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the burden-shifting premise fails, the summary-judgment attack fails with it.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a strong procedural counter. Dresher and Vahila do not require magic words, and a movant need not negate every conceivable factual dispute; it must identify record material showing the absence of a genuine issue on an essential element. The brief overstates the defect by focusing on the absence of an express statement that there is "no genuine issue as to any material fact." That is not, by itself, enough to defeat summary judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not contend that Appellee was required to utter talismanic words. Rather, under Dresher and Vahila, Appellee was required to point to record evidence showing the absence of a genuine issue on the material facts controlling its claim. Here, the record contains evidence that Appellee received rent from Wilson or his corporation and that Ruth Gross became aware Dr. Todd Wilson had entered into possession of the subject premises. Construed most strongly in Appellants' favor, that evidence creates a genuine issue whether Appellee acquiesced in the assignment and whether rent remained due from Appellants.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Remove the argument that Appellee had to use magic words or negate every conceivable factual issue. Recast the point under Dresher and Vahila as a failure to point to record material that eliminated the genuine dispute over the facts that actually mattered.

challenges.opponent_argument: Even taking Appellants’ rent-payment narrative at face value, receipt of checks from Wilson or his corporation does not automatically establish waiver or estoppel. The waiver authorities the brief relies on turn on rent acceptance with knowledge of the relevant breach or termination; the jump from "different payor" to "waiver as a matter of law" is unsupported. At most, the payments create an inference issue, not the dispositive waiver Appellants claim.
challenges.why_it_matters: If rent acceptance alone is insufficient, the assignment/waiver theory cannot defeat summary judgment on its own.
